items.title: 2.3.2 Relation between ionization energy and energy levels (electronic shells)

source_refs.note: Topic 2.3.2, printed pages 27-29: successive and first ionization energies as evidence for shells (Figures 2.4 and 2.5), with Quick Check 2.2's table read in the lesson.

blocks.text: A major difference between the electrons in different shells is their energy, so the electronic configuration of atoms can be investigated by measuring the energies of the electrons in them, which is done by measuring ionization energies. They are used in two ways: the successive ionization energies of the same element, and the first ionization energies of different elements.
Successive ionization energies of the same element

The energy required to remove each electron of an atom, one by one, can be measured: X gives X+ + e- (delta H i1), X+ gives X2+ + e- (delta H i2), X2+ gives X3+ + e- (delta H i3), and so on until only the nucleus is left. This sequence is the successive ionization energies, and it shows clearly the arrangement of electrons in shells. For magnesium, a plot of the successive ionization energies against the number of electrons removed shows the values increasing as we move from the valence shell to the inner shells. The first two electrons come from the outermost shell and need little energy, but a large increase occurs when the third is removed, because after the two outer electrons are gone the next must come from a shell much closer to the nucleus. The next seven electrons are removed from the second shell with a gradual increase, and a similar but far larger jump occurs when the eleventh and twelfth electrons are removed from the first, innermost shell next to the nucleus. The two large jumps are very good evidence that the electrons of magnesium exist in three different shells.
First ionization energies of different atoms

The second way is to look at how the first ionization energies of the elements vary with atomic number; a plot for the first 88 elements shows the following. All ionization energies are strongly endothermic: it takes energy to separate an electron from an atom. Down a group, for example helium to neon to argon or lithium to sodium to potassium, the ionization energies decrease: the larger the atom, the easier it is to separate an electron, because down the group the number of shells increases and the hold of the nucleus on the valence electrons decreases. Across a period the ionization energies generally increase: the alkali metals of group 1 have the lowest in each period and the noble gases the highest, because the shell number stays the same while the proton number increases, electrons are added to the same shell and the nucleus attracts the valence electrons more strongly.

blocks.alt: Left: dots of the successive ionization energies of magnesium rising in three steps, two low blue dots, eight green dots rising gradually, and two red dots far above, with the two jumps marked. Right: a red zigzag of first ionization energy against atomic number for the first twenty elements with peaks at He, Ne and Ar and troughs at Li, Na and K.
blocks.caption: Successive ionization energies of magnesium and first ionization energies against atomic number (original diagram after Figures 2.4 and 2.5; heights schematic).
blocks.long_description: Magnesium's twelve electrons come off in three groups: two cheaply from the third shell, then a jump, eight from the second shell with a gradual rise, then a far bigger jump for the last two next to the nucleus, which proves the three shells. The first ionization energies of successive elements rise across each period to the noble gas and fall back at the next alkali metal, and fall down any group as shells are added and the nucleus's hold weakens.
